```{r setup, include=FALSE}

  fig.height = 4.5, dpi = 144, out.width = "100%", dev = "svglite", fig.ext = "svg",

PAL <- c(blue = "#2E6F9E", red = "#B5342B", green = "#3F7A3D",
         orange = "#9E5E0F", purple = "#7A4F9E", teal = "#2A7A7A",
         grey = "#5C6166")
library(ggplot2)
library(ggplot3d)
theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 17) + theme(
  plot.background = element_rect(fill = "transparent", colour = NA),
  panel.background = element_rect(fill = "transparent", colour = NA),
  legend.background = element_rect(fill = "transparent", colour = NA),
  legend.key = element_rect(fill = "transparent", colour = NA),
  legend.box.background = element_rect(fill = "transparent", colour = NA),
  legend.position = "none"))
```

Visibility determines which parts of three-dimensional geometry can be seen from a camera. This article explains overlapping surfaces, drawing order and finite-width strokes. Installation is covered in [Get started](ggplot3d.html).

```{r}
```

## Overlapping geometry

Occlusion occurs when nearer geometry covers farther geometry in the projected image. A panel scene combines geometry from its three-dimensional layers before resolving visibility. An intersection can make different parts of a surface lie in front of and behind another surface.

```{r crossing, fig.alt="Two intersecting planes, each covering part of the other in the projected view."}
a <- expand.grid(x = seq(-1, 1, length.out = 8),
                 y = seq(-1, 1, length.out = 8))
a$z <- a$x
b <- a
b$z <- -b$x
ggplot(a, aes(x, y, z = z)) +
  geom_surface_3d(fill = PAL["blue"]) +
  geom_surface_3d(data = b, fill = PAL["orange"]) + coord_3d(elevation = 60)
```

Camera projection places the scene's faces, strokes, point marks and text on the page and assigns their depth along the viewing direction. Visibility refers to this represented geometry, including the triangles used to approximate a curved surface.

## The occlusion graph

An occlusion graph records drawing dependencies. Each node represents a piece of geometry. A directed edge says that one piece must be drawn before another where their projected areas overlap. Following these dependencies produces an order from the back of the scene towards the camera.

Some configurations create a cycle: A covers part of B, B covers part of C, and C covers part of A. Intersections can also require a change of drawing order within a face. Splitting the affected geometry supplies smaller pieces that can be ordered. Geometry whose overlap relationships already admit an order can stay intact.

The vector renderer uses this ordering and localized splitting to draw the scene. This belongs to the family of visibility methods discussed by Snyder and Lengyel [1998](https://doi.org/10.1145/280814.280878). Their paper studies visibility ordering and compositing for image layers. It provides background for thinking about occlusion dependencies.

## Splitting geometry

Splitting inserts vertices where geometry crosses a dividing plane. The resulting pieces preserve the represented surface. The classical hidden-surface method of Newell, Newell and Sancha [1972](https://doi.org/10.1145/800193.569954) and the spatial partitioning method of Fuchs, Kedem and Naylor [1980](https://doi.org/10.1145/800250.807481) establish related approaches to obtaining a visible drawing order.

Localized splitting limits the extra geometry to relationships that need it, though a dense collection of interpenetrating shapes may still require many pieces. Choose the raster backend in [Output backends](backends.html) when the intended output is a fixed-size image of dense geometry.

## Strokes and marks

A stroke covers an area determined by its width, joins and end caps. Its visible area can extend on either side of the path coordinates. Nehab [2020](https://doi.org/10.1145/3386569.3392392) explains how stroked paths define filled regions and why joins and caps matter.

Point marks also have a footprint on the page. Visibility near the boundary of a surface therefore depends on the mark's size. Physical output dimensions affect these footprints, so inspect the plot at its intended size.

```{r strokes, fig.alt="A blue surface with red observations and vertical black segments extending through it."}
points <- data.frame(x = c(-0.5, 0, 0.5), y = c(0, 0.5, 0),
                     z = c(0.6, -0.4, 0.7))
ggplot(a, aes(x, y, z = z)) + geom_surface_3d(fill = PAL["blue"]) +
  geom_segment_3d(data = points, aes(xend = x, yend = y, zend = -1),
                  linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point_3d(data = points, size = 4, colour = PAL["red"]) +
  coord_3d(elevation = 60)
```

## Feature lines and haloes

A surface or mesh layer can derive its own lines with `outline = outline_3d()`: silhouettes, where the surface turns away from the camera, creases, where neighbouring faces meet at a sharp angle, and boundaries of open surfaces. Silhouettes depend on the camera, so they are recomputed for each panel. Bénard and Hertzmann [2019](https://doi.org/10.1561/0600000075) describe these lines and how to extract them from a mesh.

The lines are strokes of the scene, so nearer surfaces hide them like any other stroke, and `hidden = "dashed"` draws their hidden parts dashed. Where a hidden line passes behind a visible one, the two strokes touch on the page and the depth order is hard to read. `halo` leaves a gap of the given width on each side of every line where a farther line passes behind it, the haloed lines of Appel, Rohlf and Stein (1979). Lines that end at a common vertex, such as the edges at a corner of a cube, still meet.

```{r halo, fig.alt="A wire-frame cube whose hidden edges are dashed and stop short of the visible edges they pass behind."}
cube <- expand.grid(x = 0:1, y = 0:1, z = 0:1)
quads <- rbind(c(1, 3, 4, 2), c(5, 6, 8, 7), c(1, 2, 6, 5),
               c(3, 7, 8, 4), c(1, 5, 7, 3), c(2, 4, 8, 6))
ggplot() +
  geom_mesh_3d(vertices = cube, faces = quads, fill = "grey95",
               outline = outline_3d(hidden = "dashed", linewidth = 0.8,
                                    halo = grid::unit(1.2, "mm"))) +
  coord_3d(azimuth = -50, elevation = 25)
```

## Transparency and overlays

An opacity below one lets farther geometry contribute to the image. The order of contributions affects the resulting colour. Exact geometric ordering describes the represented shapes; finite raster sampling and device antialiasing also affect boundary pixels.

The layer adapter accepts `occlusion = "overlay"` for geometry intended to be drawn above the depth-tested scene. Use that setting for annotations whose role requires them to remain visible.

* Newell, M. E., Newell, R. G. and Sancha, T. L. (1972). A Solution to the Hidden Surface Problem. ACM Annual Conference, 443-450. [doi:10.1145/800193.569954](https://doi.org/10.1145/800193.569954).

* Fuchs, H., Kedem, Z. M. and Naylor, B. F. (1980). On Visible Surface Generation by A Priori Tree Structures. SIGGRAPH, 124-133. [doi:10.1145/800250.807481](https://doi.org/10.1145/800250.807481).

* Bénard, P. and Hertzmann, A. (2019). Line Drawings from 3D Models: A Tutorial. Foundations and Trends in Computer Graphics and Vision 11, 1-159. [doi:10.1561/0600000075](https://doi.org/10.1561/0600000075).

* Appel, A., Rohlf, F. J. and Stein, A. J. (1979). The Haloed Line Effect for Hidden Line Elimination. SIGGRAPH '79. [history.siggraph.org](https://history.siggraph.org/?p=104577).

* Nehab, D. (2020). Converting Stroked Primitives to Filled Primitives. ACM Transactions on Graphics 39(4). [doi:10.1145/3386569.3392392](https://doi.org/10.1145/3386569.3392392).
